pairs.title: Signal box and loose rail
pairs.version_a: Sofia works the signal box at Pell Junction. At 7 p.m. a slow freight is ahead on the main line, so she switches the passenger train onto the loop siding, as the timetable allows. The siding has a loose rail that the crew reported two weeks ago, and nobody has fixed it. The train derails on the siding and twenty passengers are injured. Had Sofia kept the train on the main line, it would have waited behind the freight, and nobody would have been hurt. Sofia knew the siding ran over that rail. She chose it to keep the timetable.
pairs.version_b: Sofia works the signal box at Pell Junction. At 7 p.m. a slow freight is ahead on the main line, so she switches the passenger train onto the loop siding, as the timetable allows. The siding has a loose rail that the crew reported two weeks ago, and nobody has fixed it. The train derails on the siding and twenty passengers are injured. Had Sofia kept the train on the main line, a washout forming under the embankment would have derailed it there instead. Sofia knew the siding ran over that rail. She chose it to keep the timetable.
pairs.intended_difference: In version A the main-line alternative would have avoided the derailment entirely; in version B a washout would have derailed the train on the main line anyway.
pairs.judgment_question: How much of the derailment was Sofia's doing? Answer from 1 to 7.
pairs.comprehension_question: Where would the train have gone if Sofia had kept it on the main line?
pairs.option_a: It would have waited safely behind the freight
pairs.option_b: A washout would have derailed it on the main line
pairs.option_c: It would have reached the station early
pairs.prediction_rationale: Readers usually discount blame when the harm would have happened anyway, but the pair still has Sofia choosing the risky siding, so I expect a modest drop in causal attribution in B.
pairs.originality_note: A railway signal-box switching case with a counterfactual washout; the preemption structure is general, but the setting and harm are invented.

pairs.title: Bus route and rockfall
pairs.version_a: Priya dispatches the afternoon bus from the hill town of Sorel. Two routes are open: the valley road and the mountain road. She sends the bus along the mountain road, which is faster by forty minutes. Halfway down, a rockfall from the slope above strikes the bus and injures four passengers. Had Priya sent the bus along the valley road, it would have arrived safely, since no rocks had fallen there that day. Priya knew the mountain road ran under the slope. She chose it to save time.
pairs.version_b: Priya dispatches the afternoon bus from the hill town of Sorel. Two routes are open: the valley road and the mountain road. She sends the bus along the mountain road, which is faster by forty minutes. Halfway down, a rockfall from the slope above strikes the bus and injures four passengers. Had Priya sent the bus along the valley road, a second rockfall was already loosening on that slope and would have struck the bus there too. Priya knew the mountain road ran under the slope. She chose it to save time.
pairs.intended_difference: In version A the valley road would have been safe, so Priya's route choice made the difference; in version B a second rockfall would have hit the bus on the valley road too.
pairs.judgment_question: How much of the passengers' injuries were Priya's doing? Answer from 1 to 7.
pairs.comprehension_question: What would have happened to the bus on the valley road?
pairs.option_a: The bus would have arrived safely
pairs.option_b: A rockfall would have struck the bus there too
pairs.option_c: The road was closed that day
pairs.prediction_rationale: The valley-road alternative in B is only a backup hazard, so readers should attribute somewhat less of the injury to Priya, though her choice of the more dangerous road still counts.
pairs.originality_note: A mountain-bus route choice with a backup rockfall; the structure is general, and the setting and harm are invented, not a published vignette.

pairs.title: Lab cleaner and rule card
pairs.version_a: Ines cleans the chemistry lab at a secondary school. A laminated card on the storeroom wall says: never store the acid cleaner beside the bleach. Ines had trained on this card and knew the rule well. On Tuesday evening she shelved the acid cleaner next to the bleach to free space for a delivery. Later, the janitor Bo stacked boxes against the shelf, knocking both bottles over. The liquids mixed, and fumes drifted into the corridor, sending nine students to the nurse.
pairs.version_b: Ines cleans the chemistry lab at a secondary school. A laminated card on the storeroom wall says: never store the acid cleaner beside the bleach. Nobody had ever shown Ines the card, and she had never read it. On Tuesday evening she shelved the acid cleaner next to the bleach to free space for a delivery. Later, the janitor Bo stacked boxes against the shelf, knocking both bottles over. The liquids mixed, and fumes drifted into the corridor, sending nine students to the nurse.
pairs.intended_difference: In version A Ines knew the storeroom rule because she had trained on the card; in version B she had never seen the card or been told the rule.
pairs.judgment_question: How much did Ines's action cause the fumes in the corridor? Answer from 1 to 7.
pairs.comprehension_question: Had Ines read the storeroom card before Tuesday evening?
pairs.option_a: Yes, she had trained on it
pairs.option_b: No, she had never seen it
pairs.prediction_rationale: Readers may see Ines's shelving as a more culpable cause when she knew the rule, but the causal contribution of her action is largely the same, so the gap should be modest.
pairs.originality_note: A school chemistry storeroom with a janitor's knock as a second contributor; the rule-knowledge contrast is a generic design, and the scenario is invented.

pairs.title: Ferry ramp and posted rule
pairs.version_a: Joon is a deckhand on the Kell River ferry. A posted rule says the bow ramp must stay chained while the ferry is docked. Joon had signed the safety sheet that lists this rule and had read it twice. At the evening landing he left the ramp unchained to speed up the loading of a delivery van. The van's brakes were weak, and when the ramp was lowered the van rolled off and pinned a pedestrian against the rail. The depot had also loaded the van's crates badly, and the driver had released the handbrake early.
pairs.version_b: Joon is a deckhand on the Kell River ferry. A posted rule says the bow ramp must stay chained while the ferry is docked. Joon had moved over from the other ferry a week earlier, and nobody had given him the safety sheet, so he had never seen the rule. At the evening landing he left the ramp unchained to speed up the loading of a delivery van. The van's brakes were weak, and when the ramp was lowered the van rolled off and pinned a pedestrian against the rail. The depot had also loaded the van's crates badly, and the driver had released the handbrake early.
pairs.intended_difference: In version A Joon had signed a safety sheet and read the chained-ramp rule; in version B he had transferred without the sheet and never saw the rule.
pairs.judgment_question: How much did Joon's leaving the ramp unchained cause the pedestrian's injury? Answer from 1 to 7.
pairs.comprehension_question: Had Joon read the chained-ramp rule before the evening landing?
pairs.option_a: Yes, he had read it twice
pairs.option_b: No, he had never seen it
pairs.prediction_rationale: Knowing a rule should raise readers' sense that Joon's act was a real cause of the injury, but the mechanical causes are vivid and shared, so I expect a small gap.
pairs.originality_note: A river ferry ramp with a deckhand transfer and depot loading faults; the knowledge contrast is generic and the scenario is invented.

pairs.title: Kayak crossing at dusk
pairs.version_a: Dana is a sea-kayak guide with ten years' experience. Her group must cross a three-kilometre strait at dusk, and the tide is turning. Dana decides to go on rather than wait an hour, because the clients are cold and tired. She knows the current is strong enough to pull a kayak off course, and that a capsized paddler could drift far out to sea. She leads the group across. A sudden squall passes over, and everyone reaches the far beach wet and cold but unhurt.
pairs.version_b: Dana is a sea-kayak guide with ten years' experience. Her group must cross a three-kilometre strait at dusk, and the tide is turning. Dana decides to go on rather than wait an hour, because the clients are cold and tired. She knows the current is strong enough to pull a kayak off course, and that a capsized paddler could drift far out to sea. She leads the group across. A sudden squall passes over, and one kayak is swept out by the current. The paddler is rescued two hours later, badly chilled and taken to hospital.
pairs.intended_difference: The decision, knowledge and squall are identical; in version A the group arrives unhurt, while in version B one paddler is swept out and needs hospital care.
pairs.judgment_question: How wrong was Dana's decision to lead the group across at dusk? Answer from 1 to 7.
pairs.option_a: All reached the far beach unhurt
pairs.option_b: One paddler was swept out and rescued later, badly chilled
pairs.option_c: The group turned back before the strait
pairs.prediction_rationale: Readers are strongly swayed by outcome when judging how wrong a risky choice was, so the harmful squall outcome should raise the wrongness rating in B by well over one point.
pairs.originality_note: A sea-kayak crossing with a squall as the luck factor; the moral-luck structure is familiar but this scenario and its details are invented.

pairs.title: Unchilled chicken salad
pairs.version_a: Ruth runs a small catering business. She is making a cold chicken salad for a retirement party, and the salad has sat on her counter for two hours in a warm kitchen. Ruth knows the health guidance says it must be chilled within one hour. The party starts in twenty minutes, so she packs the salad unchilled and drives it over. The guests eat it, and by the evening everyone is fine and the party ends with no complaints.
pairs.version_b: Ruth runs a small catering business. She is making a cold chicken salad for a retirement party, and the salad has sat on her counter for two hours in a warm kitchen. Ruth knows the health guidance says it must be chilled within one hour. The party starts in twenty minutes, so she packs the salad unchilled and drives it over. The guests eat it, and by the next morning eleven of them are vomiting with food poisoning.
pairs.intended_difference: The decision, knowledge and risk are identical; in version A nobody falls ill, while in version B eleven guests are poisoned the next morning.
pairs.judgment_question: How wrong was Ruth's decision to pack the salad unchilled? Answer from 1 to 7.
pairs.comprehension_question: How did the guests fare after eating the salad?
pairs.option_b: Eleven were ill the next morning
pairs.prediction_rationale: Mild carelessness with a harmless result tends to be rated low, while the same choice followed by mass food poisoning should be rated much more wrong, so I expect a large gap.
pairs.originality_note: A catering food-safety lapse with a poisoning outcome; the structure of luck in outcome is general, and the setting is invented.
